artworks.title: Selene and Endymion
artworks.description: Poussin's Detroit canvas: the moon goddess descends in her chariot toward the sleeping shepherd — Selene's nightly love staged as cool classical theatre.

artworks.title: Selene and Endymion
artworks.description: Lairesse's Rijksmuseum overmantel: Cupid's torch leads Selene to Endymion while the moon breaks through cloud — lunar desire painted for a royal bedchamber.

artworks.title: Selene and Endymion
artworks.description: Bolognese Rococo: Selene leans from the night sky over the eternally sleeping youth — the moon's visit rendered as soft flesh and silver light.

artworks.title: Selene
artworks.description: Aublet's fin-de-siècle moon goddess — Selene alone as luminous nude against the dark, crescent and night condensed into one figure.

artworks.title: Endymion and Selene
artworks.description: Pollet's academic nocturne: Selene arrives at the sleeping shepherd — nineteenth-century polish on the oldest lunar love story.

popCulture.title: Hades II
popCulture.creator: Supergiant Games
popCulture.description: Supergiant brings Selene among the surface boons — the moon's silver light as a gift for Melinoë's night war.

popCulture.title: Endymion
popCulture.creator: John Keats
popCulture.description: Keats' long poem opens on Selene's sleeping shepherd — 'A thing of beauty is a joy for ever' — the moon's love written as Romantic quest.

popCulture.title: Endymion (mythology)
popCulture.description: The eternally sleeping youth on Mount Latmus remains Selene's defining myth — every later Diana-and-Endymion retelling still begins with her nightly descent.

popCulture.title: Luna (goddess)
popCulture.description: Rome's Luna is Selene under a Latin name — the moon goddess whose chariot still crosses Latin poetry and calendar lore.
